unit.unitTitle: Decomposing Problems: Creating a Smart Solution
unit.unitOverview: In this unit — Decomposing Problems: Creating a Smart Solution — you will work through smart devices and sensors, hardware, software and simulators, meet the micro:bit, decomposition — breaking the problem down, your first micropython program, inputs and the 'while true' loop, selection — making decisions with if and else, using the sensors in code, data types — strings and integers, more than one input and output, flowcharts and algorithm tracing, testing with a test plan and the project plan and evaluating. concepts.title: Smart Devices and Sensors
concepts.explanation:
A smart device has a program that tells it how to behave, and it uses sensors to gather data about the world. A sensor is simply a part that can detect something — light, heat, movement, sound or touch — and turn it into data (a number) that the program can use.

Think about the automatic lights in a public washroom. When you walk in, the lights come on. When you leave, they switch off after a while. Nobody flicks a switch. Inside the device is a motion sensor that detects movement, and a program that says: IF movement is detected THEN switch the light on.

Here is another example you can picture. A central-heating system uses a thermostat, which is a device with a built-in temperature sensor. The program keeps asking one question over and over: IF the temperature is below the set value THEN turn the heating on; otherwise turn it off. The sensor never stops checking, so the room stays comfortable without anyone touching a dial. When a device runs itself like this, based on sensor data, we say it is automated.

A step-counter (pedometer) in a phone or watch does not really count your legs moving.
concepts.example: It uses an accelerometer — a movement sensor — to feel the little bounce of each step, and a program counts those bounces. You will build something very similar later in this unit.

concepts.title: Hardware, Software and Simulators
concepts.explanation:
The easiest way to remember the difference between hardware and software is this: you can touch hardware, but you cannot touch software. The micro:bit itself, its buttons and its LED lights are hardware. The MicroPython program you write is software. A computing device needs both to do anything useful.

There are two families of software:

Systems software keeps the device working. The main example is the operating system (such as Windows, Linux, macOS, Android or iOS). It starts the moment you switch a device on and connects the hardware to the programs you run.

Applications software helps you complete a particular task. A web browser, a word processor, and the python.microbit.org editor are all applications. Software that does many jobs, like a word processor, is called a general-purpose application.
concepts.example: A simulator is a special kind of application that behaves like a real system so you can practise safely. Pilots learn in flight simulators before flying a real plane. Surgeons practise operations on simulators before working with a real patient. In the same way, the micro:bit simulator lets you test your program on screen before you ever touch the physical device — so a mistake costs you nothing but a moment to fix it.

concepts.title: Meet the micro:bit
concepts.explanation:
The BBC micro:bit is a pocket-sized computer built to teach you how hardware and software work together. Despite its size, it is packed with inputs and outputs. An input is data coming IN to the device; an output is something the device sends OUT to you.

Here are the main inputs and outputs you will use:

Notice how many of these are sensors. That is what makes the micro:bit perfect for building a smart device: it can sense light, heat, movement, sound and touch, and then respond using its display and speaker.

Feature — Input or Output? · What it does

Button A and Button B — Input · Two press-buttons on the front.

Touch logo — Input · The gold logo at the top can sense a finger touch (micro:bit V2).

Light sensor — Input · The LED display can also measure how bright the room is.

Temperature sensor — Input · Built into the processor; reads temperature in degrees Celsius.

Accelerometer — Input · Detects movement, tilt and gestures such as a shake.

Microphone — Input · Detects sound; can tell loud from quiet (micro:bit V2).

Compass — Input · Detects the direction the micro:bit is pointing.

LED display — Output · A 5x5 grid of 25 red lights that shows images, letters and scrolling text.
concepts.example: Speaker / buzzer — Output · Plays tunes and sounds (micro:bit V2 has a built-in speaker).

concepts.title: Decomposition - Breaking the Problem Down
concepts.explanation:
Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts. It is the skill professional programmers use every single day, because small parts are easy to understand, easy to solve, and easy to test. When you put all the small solutions together, you have solved the big problem.

Let us decompose your Final Project scenario: 'Build a device that warns the class when someone is taking a computer.' On its own, that sounds hard. But watch what happens when we break it down:

Choose the input. Which sensor will notice a thief — touch, light, or movement?

Decide the question. What exactly are we testing? For example: 'Is the logo being touched?'

Choose the outputs. What should happen on a yes? A warning image? A loud sound? Both?

Plan the flow. Draw a flowchart showing the yes path and the no path.

Write the code. Turn each flowchart step into a line of MicroPython.

Test it. Try many inputs on the simulator and check the outputs are correct.
concepts.example: Each of those six parts is small enough to finish in a few minutes. That is the magic of decomposition: a project that felt impossible becomes a short to-do list. Keep this habit for the whole unit — whenever something feels too big, break it into smaller pieces.

concepts.title: Your First MicroPython Program
concepts.explanation:
Every micro:bit program must begin by importing the micro:bit library. A library is a ready-made list of all the commands you are allowed to use. The very first line is always the same:

The star (*) means 'import everything to do with the micro:bit'. Without this line the program would not know what display, button_a or temperature mean. Now let us make the display do something. Type this program, replacing Maya with your own name:

Click the play button and watch the simulator. What happens: the word 'Maya' scrolls across the 25 LEDs one letter at a time, from right to left. As soon as the word finishes, a smiling face appears and stays lit. You have just controlled real hardware with two lines of code!
concepts.example: Two commands did all the work. display.scroll('...') slides text across the screen, and display.show(Image.HAPPY) shows a single picture that stays on. Notice that the text 'Maya' has quotation marks around it, but Image.HAPPY does not — and HAPPY is in capital letters. Those are rules of the syntax, and MicroPython is very strict about them.

concepts.title: Inputs and the 'while True' Loop
concepts.explanation:
So far the program ran once and stopped. A smart device must keep watching for input forever. To do that we wrap our code in a while True loop. Everything indented underneath it repeats again and again, for as long as the device is on. This is how the micro:bit 'constantly checks' its sensors.

What happens: the program loops forever. On each loop it asks, 'Is button A being pressed right now?' Nothing shows until you click button A on the simulator. The moment you do, 'Hello' scrolls and then a happy face appears. This is your first program with an input (the button) and an output (the display).
concepts.example: Look closely at the indentation — the spaces at the start of the lines. The code inside the loop is indented four spaces. The code inside the IF is indented four spaces again. MicroPython uses this indentation to know what belongs inside what. Getting it wrong is one of the most common beginner mistakes, so line your code up carefully.

concepts.title: Selection - Making Decisions with IF and ELSE
concepts.explanation:
Selection is how a program makes a choice. It asks a question, and depending on the answer it follows one path or another. In MicroPython the question begins with if, and the 'otherwise' path begins with else. To ask the question we compare two values using a comparison operator.

Here are the comparison operators you will use again and again:

Notice that == (two equals signs) means 'is equal to', which is a question. A single = means 'store this value', which is a command. Mixing them up is a classic bug, so read them carefully. Here is selection with a light sensor:

What happens: the light sensor reads a number from 0 (very dark) to 255 (very bright). IF the room is dark (below 100), a square lights up — like a lamp switching on. ELSE (when it is bright enough) the display clears. On the simulator, drag the light level slider down and watch the square appear, then drag it up and watch it vanish. Changing the operator would change the whole behaviour — that is why choosing the right one matters so much.

Sometimes you want to check a second, different question. For that you can use elif (short for 'else if'). The program checks the first question; if it is false it checks the elif; and if all of them are false it does the else. You will use elif in your Final Project to handle two sensors at once.

Operator — Meaning · Example

< — less than · if temperature() < 20

> — greater than · if temperature() > 35

<= — less than or equal to · if light <= 10

>= — greater than or equal to · if light >= 128

== — equal to (are they the same?) · if answer == 5

concepts.title: Using the Sensors in Code
concepts.explanation:
Now for the exciting part — reading real sensor data. Each sensor has its own command. Here are the five you will use most, each shown in a short, working program.

Temperature sensor — a hot-afternoon alert

What happens: temperature() gives back a whole number of degrees Celsius. IF it is above 35 — a genuinely hot Berbera afternoon — the word 'HOT' scrolls and an angry face shows. Otherwise a happy face shows. sleep(2000) pauses for 2000 milliseconds (2 seconds) before checking again, so the display does not flicker. On the simulator, drag the temperature slider above 35 to trigger the alert.

Light sensor — detecting a shadow

You saw display.read_light_level() above. It is perfect for detecting when a hand or a person comes close, because they block the light and the reading drops. This is exactly how a simple burglar detector works.

Touch sensor — guarding the logo

What happens: IF someone touches the gold logo, a skull appears and the 'Baddy' tune plays like an alarm. Notice the new line import music at the top — sounds live in a separate library, so you must import it before you can play a tune. On the simulator, click the logo to 'touch' it.

Accelerometer — detecting a shake

What happens: the accelerometer feels movement. IF it detects a shake gesture, a tick (YES) appears. Other gestures you can name include 'up', 'down', 'left', 'right', 'face up', 'face down' and 'freefall'. On the simulator, choose 'shake' from the gesture menu. This is the same idea a step counter uses on your walk to school: each step is a little movement the accelerometer can feel.

Sound sensor — reacting to a loud noise
concepts.example: What happens: the microphone listens. IF the most recent sound was LOUD (a clap or a shout), a surprised face shows; otherwise the display clears. Notice == is used because we are asking 'is the sound event equal to LOUD?' On the simulator, use the sound-level slider to make a loud sound.

concepts.title: Data Types - Strings and Integers
concepts.explanation:
Every piece of data in a program has a type. In this unit you need two of them.

A string is text. You write it inside quotation marks, single or double: 'Hello' or "Leo". Any characters can go in a string, even numbers like 'Pass123'.

An integer is a whole number with no decimal point and no quotation marks, like 27 or 128.
concepts.example: Why does this matter? Because the data a sensor gathers is a number, and to compare it in an IF question the program must know it is a number. Happily, the micro:bit sensors give you integers automatically — temperature() gives 27, read_light_level() gives 130 — so you can compare them with operators straight away. Text that you want to display, on the other hand, must be a string with quotation marks. A quick check: when you add quotation marks around a word in the editor, the colour of the text changes. That colour change is a handy signal that you have made a string correctly.

concepts.title: More Than One Input and Output
concepts.explanation:
A real smart device rarely does just one thing. Your Final Project must use more than one input and more than one output. That is easier than it sounds — you simply stack more IF questions inside your loop, and put more than one action inside a branch.

What happens: two inputs, two different outcomes. Press A for 'Hello' and a happy face; press B for 'Goodbye' and a sad face. You can also give a single branch several outputs — an image AND a sound AND scrolling text — which is exactly what makes a good, noticeable alarm.

concepts.title: Flowcharts and Algorithm Tracing
concepts.explanation:
Before you write code, you plan it. An algorithm is your set of steps, and a flowchart is a picture of that algorithm. Planning first means you understand what the program should do before you worry about syntax, which makes finding mistakes far easier.

A flowchart uses a few simple shapes: a rounded box for Start/Stop, a rectangle for a process, a parallelogram for input/output, and a diamond for a decision (a question with a Yes path and a No path). The diamond is where selection lives.
concepts.example: Algorithm tracing means following your flowchart with a chosen input to predict the output. For example, imagine a flowchart that asks 'Is the light level 10 or below?' If you trace it with a light level of 0, you follow the Yes path to 'alarm sounds'. Trace it with 150, and you follow the No path to 'alarm off'. Tracing lets you find errors on paper, before you have written a single line of code. If your code later behaves differently from your trace, you have found a bug.

concepts.title: Testing with a Test Plan
concepts.explanation:
Testing is how you prove your program works — not by hoping, but by checking. A test plan is a table where you choose a range of inputs, write down what you EXPECT to happen, then run the program and write down what ACTUALLY happens. If the two match, the test passes.

Here is part of a test plan for a light-based alarm that should sound when the light level is 10 or below:

Good testers pick clever values, especially ones right at the boundary. Notice tests 3 and 4 use 10 and 9 — the exact edge of the condition. Those boundary tests catch the most common mistakes, like using < when you meant <=.

Test — Data entered · Expected outcome · Actual outcome · Pass/Fail

1 — Light level = 0 · Alarm sounds · Alarm sounds · Pass

2 — Light level = 150 · Alarm off · Alarm off · Pass

3 — Light level = 10 · Alarm sounds · Alarm sounds · Pass

4 — Light level = 9 · Alarm sounds · Alarm sounds · Pass

concepts.title: The Project Plan and Evaluating
concepts.explanation:
Professional software follows a project plan with five stages. You are already using every one of them in this unit:

Plan — decompose the problem and write down your success criteria (what the finished program must do).

Design — plan the steps and draw the flowchart.

Create — write or edit the program code.

Test — run a test plan with a range of inputs and check the outputs.

Evaluate — review the tests and the finished program against your success criteria.
concepts.example: Evaluation is not only for the end. You evaluate when you trace a flowchart and when you run a test. A big part of evaluating is thinking about the user — the person who will use your device. Will they understand the output? A happy face makes a user feel at ease; a sad or angry face signals a warning. The colours, images and sounds you choose all shape how the user feels, so choose them on purpose.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 1: Smart Devices and Sensors
workedExamples.prompt: What does decomposition mean? (a) Making a program faster (b) Breaking a big problem into smaller parts (c) Deleting a program (d) Adding two numbers
workedExamples.solution:
A smart device has a program that tells it how to behave, and it uses sensors to gather data about the world. A sensor is simply a part that can detect something — light, heat, movement, sound or touch — and turn it into data (a number) that the program can use.

Think about the automatic lights in a public washroom. When you walk in, the lights come on. When you leave, they switch off after a while. Nobody flicks a switch. Inside the device is a motion sensor that detects movement, and a program that says: IF movement is detected THEN switch the light on.

Here is another example you can picture. A central-heating system uses a thermostat, which is a device with a built-in temperature sensor. The program keeps asking one question over and over: IF the temperature is below the set value THEN turn the heating on; otherwise turn it off. The sensor never stops checking, so the room stays comfortable without anyone touching a dial. When a device runs itself like this, based on sensor data, we say it is automated.

A step-counter (pedometer) in a phone or watch does not really count your legs moving.

For example: It uses an accelerometer — a movement sensor — to feel the little bounce of each step, and a program counts those bounces. You will build something very similar later in this unit.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 2: Hardware, Software and Simulators
workedExamples.prompt: Which line must appear at the top of every micro:bit program? (a) import microbit (b) from microbit import * (c) start microbit (d) microbit.begin()
workedExamples.solution:
The easiest way to remember the difference between hardware and software is this: you can touch hardware, but you cannot touch software. The micro:bit itself, its buttons and its LED lights are hardware. The MicroPython program you write is software. A computing device needs both to do anything useful.

There are two families of software:

Systems software keeps the device working. The main example is the operating system (such as Windows, Linux, macOS, Android or iOS). It starts the moment you switch a device on and connects the hardware to the programs you run.

Applications software helps you complete a particular task. A web browser, a word processor, and the python.microbit.org editor are all applications. Software that does many jobs, like a word processor, is called a general-purpose application.

For example: A simulator is a special kind of application that behaves like a real system so you can practise safely. Pilots learn in flight simulators before flying a real plane. Surgeons practise operations on simulators before working with a real patient. In the same way, the micro:bit simulator lets you test your program on screen before you ever touch the physical device — so a mistake costs you nothing but a moment to fix it.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 4: Decomposition - Breaking the Problem Down
workedExamples.prompt: Explain in your own words: Decomposition — Breaking the Problem Down.
workedExamples.solution:
Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts. It is the skill professional programmers use every single day, because small parts are easy to understand, easy to solve, and easy to test. When you put all the small solutions together, you have solved the big problem.

Let us decompose your Final Project scenario: 'Build a device that warns the class when someone is taking a computer.' On its own, that sounds hard. But watch what happens when we break it down:

Choose the input. Which sensor will notice a thief — touch, light, or movement?

Decide the question. What exactly are we testing? For example: 'Is the logo being touched?'

Choose the outputs. What should happen on a yes? A warning image? A loud sound? Both?

Plan the flow. Draw a flowchart showing the yes path and the no path.

Write the code. Turn each flowchart step into a line of MicroPython.

Test it. Try many inputs on the simulator and check the outputs are correct.

For example: Each of those six parts is small enough to finish in a few minutes. That is the magic of decomposition: a project that felt impossible becomes a short to-do list. Keep this habit for the whole unit — whenever something feels too big, break it into smaller pieces.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 6: Inputs and the 'while True' Loop
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is an input? (a) The LED display (b) The speaker (c) Button A (d) The scroll command
workedExamples.solution:
So far the program ran once and stopped. A smart device must keep watching for input forever. To do that we wrap our code in a while True loop. Everything indented underneath it repeats again and again, for as long as the device is on. This is how the micro:bit 'constantly checks' its sensors.

What happens: the program loops forever. On each loop it asks, 'Is button A being pressed right now?' Nothing shows until you click button A on the simulator. The moment you do, 'Hello' scrolls and then a happy face appears. This is your first program with an input (the button) and an output (the display).

For example: Look closely at the indentation — the spaces at the start of the lines. The code inside the loop is indented four spaces. The code inside the IF is indented four spaces again. MicroPython uses this indentation to know what belongs inside what. Getting it wrong is one of the most common beginner mistakes, so line your code up carefully.

rules.text: Every program starts with: from microbit import * Image names are in CAPITALS with no quotes: Image.HEART. Text to display goes in quotation marks: 'Hello'.

Lines that end with a colon (while True: , if ... : , else:) must have indented code underneath. Indent four spaces for each step. Keep your indentation lined up. == asks a question (is it equal?). A single = stores a value.

sleep(1000) pauses for 1 second and is spelled with a lower-case s. Sensor readings are integers (whole numbers), so you can compare them straight away. To play sounds you must first write: import music

Image names must be typed in CAPITAL letters and with no quotation marks: Image.HEART, Image.HAPPY, Image.SAD. Text to display must go inside quotation marks: 'Hello' or "Hello". Both single and double quotes work. If you get these wrong the program will not run — and that is normal. Every programmer fixes syntax all day.

while True: needs the colon at the end, and everything that should repeat must be indented underneath it. if button_a.is_pressed(): also needs a colon, and its actions are indented one more step. reasoningPrompts.prompt: In your own words, what is decomposition and why is it useful when planning a program?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts. It is useful because small parts are easier to understand, solve and test, so a hard project becomes a short list of simple steps.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name three sensors on the micro:bit and say what each one detects.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any three of: buttons (a press), light sensor (brightness), temperature sensor (heat), accelerometer (movement/gestures), microphone (sound), touch logo (a finger touch), compass (direction).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between an input and an output? Give one micro:bit example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: An input is data going in (for example pressing button A); an output is what the device produces (for example the LED display showing a heart, or the speaker playing a tune).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What does the while True loop do, and why do button programs need it?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: while True repeats the indented code forever. Button programs need it so the micro:bit keeps checking for a press again and again instead of checking once and stopping.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between a string and an integer, with one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A string is text inside quotation marks (for example 'Hello'); an integer is a whole number with no quotation marks (for example 27).
